# NIST SSDF v1.1 for software-business work

**Source:** Souppaya, Scarfone and Dodson (2022), *Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1*, NIST SP 800-218, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218. Scope: open. United States public domain; worldwide reprint and derivative-work permission under NIST Technical Series Publications policy. Republished courtesy of the National Institute of Standards and Technology.
**Projection:** Secure-development ownership, evidence, supplier choices and risk decisions for founders, CTOs and engineering leaders. Questions, diagnostic patterns and the worked scenario are applications authored for this task; source claims retain their evidence markers. No lens variant is applied.

## Software-Business Relevance

SSDF helps a software leader specify what secure delivery requires across the organisation, code and releases, production practices and vulnerability response. It supplies a vocabulary for relating a business commitment to requirements, accountable roles, checks, evidence and continuing response work. The source addresses producers regardless of size or maturity while explicitly distinguishing understanding its guidance from having the expertise to implement it. [AP] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, Audience, pp. iii–iv; §1, pp. 2–3; §2, p. 4)

The investment question is contextual: which practices apply, what risk do they address, and what implementation is feasible at the organisation's stage? SSDF directs attention to risk, cost, feasibility, applicability and automatability, and leaves implementation methods open. This makes it useful for a security work plan or an assurance memo whose commitments must be both operationally specific and resourced. [AR] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, §1, p. 3)

> "The focus is on the outcomes of the practices rather than on the tools, techniques, and mechanisms to do so."
>
> [V] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, Executive Summary, p. vi)

## Key Concepts for Software-Business

1. <!-- concept: risk-based-security --> **Risk-based adoption.** Decide implementation depth using risk, cost, feasibility, applicability and automatability. Examples are not mandatory, and their ordering does not establish priority. [AP] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, §1, p. 3; §2, p. 4)
2. <!-- concept: security-requirements --> **Maintained requirements.** Infrastructure, development processes and software need documented requirements that stay current; supplier requirements must also be communicated. [AP] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PO.1, pp. 5–6)
3. <!-- concept: secure-development-accountability --> **Accountability and proficiency.** Define roles, review role-based proficiency and obtain leadership commitment; the release-accountable leader/team is one notional implementation example. [AP] [AE] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PO.2, pp. 6–7)
4. <!-- concept: secure-development-toolchains --> **Maintained tools and audit artefacts.** Specify tool integration, maintain tool security and generate records of performed practices, including assigning responsibility for records tools cannot generate. [AP] [AE] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PO.3, pp. 7–8)
5. <!-- concept: software-security-checks --> **Decision criteria and supporting evidence.** Define security-check criteria and safeguard the information used; examples record approvals, rejections and exception requests. [AP] [AE] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PO.4, p. 8)
6. <!-- concept: secure-development-environments --> **Protected environments and code.** Separate/protect development environments, harden endpoints and restrict access to all code forms according to least privilege. [AP] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PO.5 and PS.1, pp. 8–9)
7. <!-- concept: software-provenance --> **Release integrity and provenance.** Provide integrity-verification information, archive releases and retain component provenance; an SBOM is a notional example of provenance data. [AP] [AE] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PS.2–PS.3, p. 10)
8. <!-- concept: threat-modelling --> **Design decisions and review.** Model security risk, retain design/risk/exception records and review design through qualified people who did not create it and/or automated processes. [AP] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PW.1–PW.2, pp. 11–12)
9. <!-- concept: security-testing --> **Production assurance across several practices.** Component verification, appropriate secure coding, secure build configuration, code review/analysis, executable tests and secure defaults are distinct SSDF practices. [AP] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PW.4–PW.9, pp. 12–16)
10. <!-- concept: vulnerability-management --> **Response and prevention of recurrence.** Gather credible reports, maintain disclosure/remediation processes, assess risk, implement responses, find recurring causes and update the SDLC. [AP] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, RV.1–RV.3, pp. 16–19)

## Questions to Ask During Software-Business

### Phase 1: Strategic positioning

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Compare build and buy with security responsibilities visible | What requirements must a component satisfy, what provenance can its supplier provide, and how will we verify it remains maintained and suitable throughout its life cycle? | [AP] [AE] PO.1.3, pp. 5–6; PW.4, pp. 12–13 |
| Bound a platform/service dependency | Which practices/tasks are ours and which are the provider's, and how will the provider attest to its part? | [AP] §1, p. 3 |

### Phase 2: Product and engineering economics

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Make a resourced security work plan | For each proposed practice, what are the risk, cost, feasibility, applicability and automation considerations, and what implementation depth are we choosing? | [AP] §1, p. 3 |
| Consider the timing of security work | Which requirements or design risks can we address now, and which would otherwise become flaws to remediate late in development or production? | [AR] §1, p. 1; [AP] PW.1, p. 11 |

### Phase 3: Team and capability building

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Assign responsibility across staff and advisers | Who owns each secure-development responsibility, who is accountable for production release, and what delegation is explicit? | [AP] [AE] PO.2.1 and PO.2.3, pp. 6–7 |
| Check capability behind a commitment | What implementation expertise does this work require, and how will we review role-based proficiency and close training gaps? | [AP] Audience, pp. iii–iv; PO.2.2, p. 6 |

### Phase 4: Operations and process

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Make tool output usable in release decisions | What security criteria does each check inform, where are findings triaged, and where do we retain approvals, rejections and exception requests? | [AP] [AE] PO.3.3–PO.4, pp. 7–8; PW.7.2, pp. 14–15 |
| Sustain the delivery controls | Who maintains the toolchain, verifies its integrity, protects its environments and supplies evidence that automation cannot produce? | [AP] [AE] PO.3.2–PO.3.3 and PO.5, pp. 7–9 |

### Phase 5: Risk, reliability, compliance

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Examine the security case for a release | What evidence covers design risks, component checks, code review/analysis, executable testing and secure defaults for this release? | [AP] PW.1–PW.2 and PW.4–PW.9, pp. 11–16 |
| Plan for a vulnerability after release | How will reports reach us, how will we assess risk and choose a response, and how will we find similar defects and change the SDLC to reduce recurrence? | [AP] RV.1–RV.3, pp. 16–19 |

### Phase 6: Stakeholder communication

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Explain assurance commitments to an executive or acquirer | Can we express requirements, owners, performed checks, retained evidence and exceptions using the same vocabulary, with each claim linked to its record? | [AP] §1, pp. 2–3; PO.1–PO.4, pp. 5–8 |
| Prepare useful vulnerability communications | Who owns the stakeholder communication plan, and how will we publish actionable advisories and deliver remediation through trusted mechanisms? | [AE] RV.1.3, p. 17; RV.2.2, p. 18 |

## What to Look For

These are task applications of the cited guidance, not additional findings attributed to NIST.

- **Checks without a decision process.** Signal: tools report findings, but the release discussion cannot identify criteria, triage or exceptions. Diagnosis: the discussion has not connected toolchain evidence to PO.4's security decisions. Follow-up: identify the criteria, evidence location and approvals/rejections/exception-request records. [AP] [AE] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PO.3.3–PO.4, pp. 7–8)
- **An adviser relationship with unassigned work.** Signal: the team names an expert but cannot say which tasks the person owns or reviews. Diagnosis: PO.2 responsibilities and capability need to be made explicit. Follow-up: map roles, training/proficiency and release accountability; specify the chosen design-review method. [AP] [AE] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PO.2, pp. 6–7; PW.2, p. 12)
- **A release record that cannot identify its components.** Signal: an older release exists but its component provenance is unavailable or stale. Diagnosis: the evidence needed for the PS.3 provenance practice is missing from the review. Follow-up: establish the release archive and maintained provenance, then use them in ongoing vulnerability work. [AP] [AE] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PS.3, p. 10; RV.1, pp. 16–17)
- **A repeated defect with only repeated fixes.** Signal: similar vulnerabilities recur while each is treated independently. Diagnosis: RV.3's pattern, class-wide and SDLC feedback questions have not been answered. Follow-up: examine shared causes, similar vulnerable code and the manual/toolchain changes that could prevent recurrence. [AP] [AE] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, RV.3, pp. 18–19)

## When to Use This Reference

- A founder or CTO needs a concrete secure-development work plan spanning roles, infrastructure, code, release integrity and response. [AP] (§2, p. 4; PO, PS, PW and RV)
- A supplier or platform decision needs requirements and responsibility boundaries. [AP] (§1, p. 3; PO.1.3, pp. 5–6; PW.4, pp. 12–13)
- A release or assurance memo needs to connect tools and evidence to explicit security-check criteria. [AP] (PO.3–PO.4, pp. 7–8)
- Vulnerability remediation needs to produce learning and prevention as well as a fix. [AP] (RV.2–RV.3, pp. 17–19)

## Worked Example

**Illustrative scenario authored for this projection:** A small software company is preparing a customer pilot. The team has code scanning and dependency alerts, an external security adviser and a target launch date. The founder is preparing a secure-delivery plan for the leadership team.

The founder first records applicable security requirements and the division of responsibility among the company, adviser and service providers; named roles and implementation expertise become concrete inputs to the plan. [AP] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, Audience, pp. iii–iv; §1, p. 3; PO.1–PO.2, pp. 5–7)

The team then connects each chosen tool/check to a criterion and retained evidence, identifies records that tools cannot generate, and records its approvals, rejections and exception requests. [AP] [AE] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PO.3.3–PO.4, pp. 7–8)

Design risks and decisions, the chosen design-review mechanism, component verification, code review/analysis, executable tests and secure defaults become separate topics in the release discussion; integrity information and provenance accompany the archived release. [AP] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, PW.1–PW.2, PW.4–PW.9, pp. 11–16; PS.2–PS.3, p. 10)

Finally, the plan states how the team receives reports, chooses risk responses and changes development practices when causes recur. [AP] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, RV.1–RV.3, pp. 16–19)

The founder uses local risk, feasibility and cost to select the implementation depth and sequence, preserving the source's central constraint:

> "The intention of the SSDF is not to create a checklist to follow, but to provide a basis for planning and implementing a risk-based approach to adopting secure software development practices."
>
> [V] (Source: Souppaya et al., SSDF v1.1, §1, p. 3)

## Anti-patterns This Reference Helps Avoid

| Signal | Diagnosis | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| The team treats every notional example as mandatory | Examples are being converted into requirements the source does not impose. [AP] (§2, p. 4) | Record the applicable outcome and chosen implementation, with risk/cost/feasibility reasoning. [AP] (§1, p. 3) |
| Buying a tool ends the security-work conversation | The adoption plan has left maintenance, evidence and criteria unspecified. [AP] (PO.3–PO.4, pp. 7–8) | Assign toolchain maintenance and evidence responsibilities, then define decision criteria. [AP] (PO.3–PO.4, pp. 7–8) |
| Developer self-review is presented as the whole code-review process | The cited notional example treats self-review as a complement to review by others or tools. [AE] (PW.5.1, p. 13) | State which review/analysis method is selected and where findings are recorded and triaged. [AP] (PW.7, pp. 14–15) |
| Work stops at publication of the release | The plan has not assigned ongoing vulnerability work. [AP] (RV.1–RV.3, pp. 16–19) | Specify reporting, response, provenance use, pattern analysis and SDLC feedback. [AP] (PS.3.2, p. 10; RV.1–RV.3, pp. 16–19) |

## Citation and Source-Integrity Notes

- **Borrowed-through gaps:** SSDF cites many other standards/guides. The NIST CSF, NICE, ISO/IEC, SAFECode, NTIA and other underlying works were not independently ingested as part of this source; their role here remains SSDF's reference mapping or attribution, not a second body of independently verified evidence. Its ASVS mapping refers to **4.0.3**, not a later edition. [BT] (SSDF deep, “Connections the author makes in the text”)
- **Named limits:** SSDF supplies high-level outcomes and a subset of what an organisation may need; it does not prescribe implementation methods, prioritise practices, require particular examples or define every contextual term. Its Audience section says expertise is required for implementation. [AP] (Audience, pp. iii–iv; §1, p. 3; §2, p. 4) This projection supplies questions and an illustrative planning scenario, not an assessment of any particular company's security or regulatory conformance.
- **Evidence-marker continuity:** [AP] records recommended practices, [AR] the authors' reasoning, [AE] notional examples and [BT] mapped/borrowed material. The two [V] passages are copied unchanged from the independently audited deep reference. Questions and diagnostic applications cite their basis without claiming that NIST observed the invented situations.
- **Audit trail:** Derived from the final cross-family-audited `nist-ssdf-1-1-deep.md`; no raw-source re-extraction occurred during projection. Open Kanban's narrow integration statement was checked against its deep-reference workflow section. The standard nine projection sections are followed by the task's runtime-trigger section.
